verses.note: Humanity alone is made after divine deliberation and in God's image. The verse defines human beings by their relation to God before anything else, and gives them a vocation: to represent God's rule over the world he made.

Man and woman bear God's image equally. Whatever else the image means, it cannot be restricted to one sex, one people, or one class, and the New Testament grounds respect for every person in it (James 3:9).
Dominion is exercised as God's image-bearers, so it has to reflect his character. Psalm 8 marvels at this calling, and Hebrews 2:5-9 says it finds its true fulfillment in Jesus.

Nefesh here is not the immortal soul of Greek philosophy but the whole living creature, made of earth and animated by God. The verse holds together frailty and dignity: dust, and yet breathed into by God. How body and soul relate, and what survives death, is taught elsewhere in Scripture and confessed by the church (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), and the final hope is bodily resurrection.

Even in a perfect garden with God present, human beings are not made to be solitary. Relationship with other people belongs to the goodness of creation, and isolation is a lack God himself names and meets.

God lets the man's naming stand. Human decisions have real weight in God's world: the dominion of 1:28 is exercised here by speech that orders and classifies, a first picture of human culture and science under God.

The man recognizes in the woman not a possession but a kinswoman of his own substance. Human sexual difference is presented as correspondence and delight, the first human speech in the Bible a cry of recognition.

Human beings remain dust, bound to the earth they came from. The New Testament's hope does not deny this but answers it with resurrection: the body sown in weakness is raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42-49).

The first murder is the killing of a brother. Scripture treats every murder in that light: 9:6 grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God, and Jesus traces murder back to anger and contempt toward a brother (Matthew 5:21-22).
Genesis restates human dignity at the head of a list of deaths. The fall has not revoked the likeness of God or the blessing of 1:28; the genealogy is how the blessing to multiply goes on working.

The image of God is passed on through ordinary human birth, which is why Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 can treat every later person as bearing it. Many interpreters add that Adam also passes on the fallen condition of chapter 3, a point Christian traditions develop differently in their teaching on original sin.

The human vocation given at creation survives the flood. Humanity's calling to fill the earth was not cancelled by sin or by judgment, which is why the Old Testament can go on to treat children and fruitfulness as gifts of God's blessing.

The image of God is not lost after the flood. Genesis 9:6 speaks of every human being, the violent ones included, as still made in God's image, and it grounds the gravity of murder there. James 3:9 makes the same argument about cursing people made in God's likeness.
Every nation descends from one family that came out of the ark. Paul makes the same point before the council of the Areopagus in Athens: God made every nation of men from one man (Acts 17:26).

Peoples at the far edge of Israel's world, horse riders from the north and Greeks across the sea, are named as members of Noah's family. Later prophets place several of them in visions of the end (Ezekiel 38:2-6; Isaiah 66:19), but here they are simply kin.

Ham's line includes Egypt, Babylon, and the Canaanites, Israel's greatest oppressors and rivals, and it is described with exactly the same words as the others. The table does not rank the three branches; each has its clans, languages, lands, and nations.

Joktan's descendants are as much Shem's children as Peleg's, yet the story will not follow them. Descent from Shem does not by itself put a people in the line of promise, and the table gives the side branch as much care as any other.
Humanity begins as one people with one speech. The unity itself is not condemned; the story will show that the problem lies in what united humanity sets out to do with it.
